analysis.one_liner: Gives people control over how companies collect, use, and sell their personal data, and adds protections for children's and teens' information online.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on May 21, 2014 and died there when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, without a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set national privacy rules for companies that collect personal information about more than 5,000 people. Companies would have to tell you what they collect and why, get your permission before using your data for advertising or sharing it with others, keep only the data they need, and tell you when a breach exposes your information — plus give you free credit reports after a big breach. It would also update the children's online privacy law to cover mobile apps, block targeted ads to kids and young teens without consent, and let young users delete personal content they posted. It never got past the introductory step: referred to committee, no cosponsors, no hearing, no vote, dead when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers: anyone who uses websites, apps, bank accounts, or credit — essentially everyone whose name, address, email, phone number, or browsing habits get collected and traded. The bill would give people the right to see and correct what companies hold on them, to opt in before their data is used for ads or sold onward, and to be told promptly when a breach exposes their information, with free credit reports afterward. Parents and teens gain specifically: targeted marketing to children and 13-to-15-year-olds would require consent, and location tracking of kids would be restricted.

how_it_helps.text: Companies would have to tell you what data they collect about you and why, and notify you before making a material change to those practices.

You would have to give opt-in consent before a company used your information in ways you did not authorize, or let third parties use it to target you with advertising — and you could access and correct the data companies store about you.

Companies could only collect and keep the personal data reasonably necessary for the service you asked for, and could not sell it onward to third parties who combine it to identify you without your consent.

After a data breach, you would be notified without unreasonable delay, given free credit reports for two years, and large breaches would be reported to federal law enforcement and state attorneys general.

The Do Not Track Kids title would ban targeted marketing to children and young teens without consent, restrict collection of their location data, and let users erase publicly posted content containing personal information.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that profit from collecting, sharing, and advertising against personal data — data brokers, ad-tech firms, and large online platforms — would bear compliance costs, consent requirements, limits on how much data they can keep and sell, and civil penalties up to $6 million per series of violations for reckless or repeat violations. Breach notification duties and free credit reports after large breaches add further cost to any company holding consumer data.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers, ad-tech, and online platforms

drawbacks.text: Companies could escape key privacy rules by joining self-policing 'safe harbor' programs run by private, often industry-affiliated organizations, approved by the FTC — weakening the mandate in practice.
The bill would have preempted (overridden) many stronger state privacy laws, potentially replacing tougher state protections with a single federal floor.

The bill explicitly provides no private right of action — individual consumers could not sue companies that violate their privacy; enforcement would depend on the FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general.

Companies could be exempt from breach notification if they conclude there is no reasonable risk of identity theft or fraud, or if they use a security program that blocks fraudulent transactions — decisions made by the company itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to ordinary people are real and substantial: fewer surprise disclosures of personal data, a legal right to correct information held about them, and honest notification when their data is stolen, with free credit monitoring after large breaches. The costs are compliance burdens on companies — but the bill scales those burdens to company size and lets small businesses seek waivers. The serious design flaws are structural: no private right of action leaves enforcement to agencies and state attorneys general; industry-run safe harbors could hollow out protections; and federal preemption would wipe out stronger state laws like California's, trading state-by-state strength for a potentially weaker national floor. A stronger version would keep those state laws and let consumers sue directly. As written, it is a genuine but imperfect privacy baseline — and the country went without even that when the bill died.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Senator Menendez on May 21, 2014 and, the same day, read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral.
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill died with it; it was not reintroduced in the record shown.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, ad-tech firms, and platforms that profit from unconsented collection of personal data kept operating under industry self-regulation.

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Commercial Privacy Bill of Rights Act of 2014 on May 21, 2014.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 21, 2014 and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the 113th Congress.

against.name: Internet, advertising, and data-broker industries
against.role: Data-driven businesses opposing federal privacy mandates
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against comprehensive federal privacy legislation during this period, preferring industry self-regulation — the very approach the bill's findings called insufficient.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other senator cosponsored the bill, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no visible partisan or bipartisan support pattern.

industries.industry: Data brokers and online advertising trackers
industries.note: Opt-in consent for third-party use of personal data and limits on combining data to identify individuals would directly cut into the business of profiling and selling consumers. The bill's own findings state that industry self-regulation had provided insufficient protection.

They would bear real compliance costs and lose access to unconsented behavioral data, but would gain uniform federal rules instead of 50 different state laws (the bill preempts most state privacy rules). Children's apps would face the strictest rules.

The bill would create a formal role for nongovernmental organizations to administer FTC-approved safe harbor programs, letting participating companies self-certify compliance — a co-regulatory structure the industry could staff and steer.

industries.industry: Credit reporting agencies and breach-prone data holders
industries.note: Mandatory breach notification, free credit reports for two years after large breaches, and penalties up to $6 million per related series of violations would raise the cost of lax security.
